newsitem.title: KENYA: U.S. says U.N. environment agency in peril.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says U.N. environment agency in peril.

text.p: The United States, taking to Africa its campaign for a shake-up of the U.N., says the world body's environment agency UNEP must be "reinvented" or face extinction.

"Today...UNEP suffers from a loss of focus, strategic vision, and influence. Instead of doing a limited number of things effectively, its work plan is disjointed and lacks clear priorities," Eileen B. Claussen, an assistant secretary of state, told the governing body of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP).
"The result is that UNEP has been marginalized to a perilous extent," Claussen, heading the U.S. delegation, said in a speech on Wednesday at the agency's headquarters in Nairobi.
The United States is leading criticism of UNEP as poorly managed and drifting into irrelevance during the global debate on how to protect the environment.
The complaint is linked to Washington's wider campaign for wholesale reform of the U.N. and its agencies.
UNEP's Canadian executive director, Elizabeth Dowdeswell, defended her record on Wednesday but announced she would not seek to extend her term when it expires at the end of 1997.

Dowdeswell told the opening ministerial session of UNEP's governing council that governments were condemning the only global U.N. agency based in the Third World to a slow death by under-funding and lack of political support.

Claussen, the text of whose speech was not available on Wednesday, said damage to the environment from causes like over-population, "greenhouse effect" gas emissions and deforestation, was continuing almost unabated.
"We must have a strong international institution for the environment and today's UNEP no longer fits that description," she said.
Claussen proposed four "core objectives" for UNEP to make it the world's leading forum on the environment and enforcer of multilateral environmental agreements.
She said the governing council should appoint an ad hoc committee to look at every aspect of UNEP and make recommendations "with an eye toward reinventing UNEP".
Claussen warned of the risks if such action was not taken to "turn UNEP around".
"...instead of leading the way into the dawn of a new and more sustainable century, UNEP will simply fade away into the dusk of this one," she said.
The new U.S.-backed secretary-general of the United Nations, Kofi Annan, has pledged to make reforms but also wants the United States to settle its debts of about $1 billion.
